transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

I keep getting stuck on how my jaw and one side of my face look—sort of sagging and uneven. It really hit me after seeing all those family photos. My wife and even my clients say they barely notice anything, but I keep seeing it.
Do you find yourself repeatedly checking your face in mirrors or other reflective surfaces?

Yes. Before client meetings, I’ll check the bathroom mirror and then my phone camera several times. I’ll mess with the lighting, change my collar, turn my face a little differently. And I end up comparing myself to younger advisors or people at gallery events instead of just focusing on who I’m talking to.
Have you been avoiding social or work situations because of how your face looks?

A little. I still make it to work and get through my appointments, but it takes me longer to get out the door for client meetings, and I’m not always fully present once I’m there. I’ve also skipped a few art openings because I didn’t want people looking at me or taking pictures.
When thoughts about your face come up, do you feel driven to do something over and over to relieve the anxiety?

Yeah. I’ll keep checking the bathroom mirror and my phone camera before meetings, trying different lighting or changing my collar, turning my face different ways. And then I start comparing myself to younger advisors or people at gallery events instead of paying attention to the conversation.
Do you think your face actually looks noticeably uneven to other people, or do you think this might be something you’re seeing more than others do?

I mean, I see this sagging, uneven look around my jaw, especially on one side. It really stood out to me in the family photos. But my wife and even clients say they barely notice anything, so… I guess it may be more obvious to me than it is to other people.
How much distress do these thoughts about your face cause you?

It’s distressing, but not overwhelming. I keep getting stuck on the sagging and unevenness around my jaw, especially since those family photos. Even though my wife and clients say they barely notice it, I can’t always let it go.
Right now, how certain are you that your face truly looks noticeably sagging or uneven to other people?

I’m not completely certain. I keep seeing the sagging and unevenness around my jaw, especially in those family photos, but my wife and clients tell me they barely notice it. So I guess it may be more noticeable to me than to other people.
Aside from your jaw and facial appearance, do you have other unwanted thoughts that keep intruding and feel hard to control?
Not really. I haven’t noticed other thoughts like that intruding or being hard to control.
On a typical day, about how much total time do you spend thinking about your jaw or checking and adjusting your appearance because of it?

Probably around client meetings, several times in a day. I’ll check the bathroom mirror and my phone camera, adjust the lighting, maybe change my collar or angle my face. And at gallery events I catch myself comparing my face to younger people instead of just focusing on the conversation.
On a typical day, do thoughts about your jaw and the checking or adjusting because of it add up to at least an hour?

Yes, I think it probably does add up to at least an hour. Before meetings I check the mirror and phone camera several times, adjust things, and then I’ll find myself comparing my face to younger people at events instead of paying attention to the conversation.
Has a doctor or dentist ever told you that there is actually noticeable sagging or asymmetry in your jaw or face?

No, I haven’t had a doctor or dentist tell me there’s anything noticeably wrong. It’s mostly something I see—this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face, especially in family photos. My wife and clients say they barely notice it.
Has worrying about your face caused problems in your work, social life, or relationships?

I still get through my work, but it has affected things some. I’m slower getting out the door for client meetings, and during a few appointments I’ve been less present than I should be. Socially, I’ve skipped a few art openings because I didn’t want to be seen or photographed.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most days?
I’m not sure I’d say depressed most days. I do get frustrated and self-conscious about my face, but I haven’t really thought of myself as feeling down all the time.
Have you noticed any actual change in your face or jaw over time that other people can clearly see?

I feel like I’ve noticed it more over time, especially in those family photos—the sagging around my jaw and one side looking uneven. But my wife and clients say they barely see anything, so I don’t know if it’s actually changed in a way other people can clearly notice.
When you’re around other people, do you worry that they’re judging you because of how your face looks?

Yeah, sometimes. I worry people are noticing the sagging around my jaw or that one side of my face looks uneven, especially after those family photos. Even though my wife and clients say they barely notice it, I still get stuck thinking other people might be judging it.
